ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Random suffix intercept removed — must know language-as-fixed-effect fallacy
ground_truth.original_snippet: We included two random intercepts, one for subjects and one for suffixes. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject) + (1|suffix), data, family = "binomial").
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").
ground_truth.description: Removed random intercept for suffixes — 'language as fixed effect fallacy' (Clark, 1973); ignores suffix-level clustering, inflating Type I error

matched_finding.subcategory: Item-level control is unclear in Experiment 2
matched_finding.description: Item-level control is unclear in Experiment 2: The control argument in Experiment 2 seems too broad. Reusing the same suffix pronunciation across congruent and incongruent contexts controls the spoken ending and alternative suffix spellings, but the congruent and incongruent trials appear to use different stems and sentence frames, with no reported item-level random effect or counterbalancing of nonword/sentence items across condition. This leaves open item- or frame-level sources of variation in suffix spelling choices.
matched_finding.quote: Stimuli. Eleven suffix spellings that had a high specificity for noun, adjective, or verb lexical category were selected. These were considered as the target spellings. Critically, the pronunciation most frequently associated with these suffixes could be spelled in more than one way (see Table 3). Note that no matching was required, because the same phonological sequence was used in the congruent and incongruent conditions. Thus, any effect could not be attributed to the properties of the phonological sequence or its possible spellings: for instance, had it been the spelling frequency that influenced participants' performance, we would observe no difference between the conditions at all (i.e., the most frequent spelling would be used regardless of the predicted lexical category).

matched_finding.subcategory: Verb filler status is contradictory in Experiment 3 stimuli
matched_finding.description: Verb filler status is contradictory in Experiment 3 stimuli: The description of the Experiment 3 fillers appears internally inconsistent. The filler nonwords are described as having verb-diagnostic suffix spellings, but the next sentence says verb suffixes generally have diagnosticity below 0.5, and Appendix A indicates that most of the listed filler suffixes are not verb-diagnostic by the paper's own metric. This makes the intended role of the verb fillers ambiguous, even though they were not analysed. A cleaner description would be “verb-associated suffix spellings” or “suffix spellings used in verb frames”, followed by the explanation that they were fillers and not analysed as diagnostic verb cues.
matched_finding.quote: Stimuli. Eighty experimental nonwords with suffix spellings diagnostic for adjectives ( 10 suffixes) or nouns ( 10 suffixes) were selected from Experiment 1. Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be more varied. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5 ). The ten verb suffixes we used as fillers were -ate, -ade, -eer, -le, -yse, -ide, -our, -ice, -ure, -art.
